summary.title: Git Merge vs. Rebase: What's the Diff?
summary.one_liner: You learn how git merge and git rebase both incorporate commits from one branch into another, how each changes history, and when to use each one.
keywords: how to keep feature branch up to date
takeaways: git merge combines two branches with a new merge commit, preserving the branch history and grouping commits together.
git rebase moves a branch's base to another commit by replaying its commits, producing a linear history with no extra commit.
Rebasing creates new commits with new SHAs and rewrites the branch history, so it can cause conflicts for others who share the branch.
Use merge to group a set of commits visibly, use rebase to keep history linear, and never rebase a public or shared branch.
summary.summary: The article walks through a tiny example website with a master branch and a feature branch, using simple diagrams of commit histories. It first shows a merge of feature into master, which creates a merge commit that groups the feature's changes, and discusses how excessive merge commits clutter logs. It then shows rebasing the feature branch onto master, which replays its commits on a new base with no extra commit, and explains the rewritten history and the risks when a collaborator shares the branch. It closes with a summary of when to merge, when to rebase, and the rule against rebasing shared branches.
